name: Light Hazel
lede: Light Hazel is ColorHub's English rendering of Aokuchiba, a traditional Japanese color whose kanji literally read "pale" and "fallen leaf."

sections.title: Pale fallen leaves
sections.body: The Japanese name is *Aokuchiba* (青朽葉), written with kanji that mean "pale fallen leaf": a muted, yellow-brown tone named for autumn foliage after its green has faded [1]. It appears among the traditional colors of Japan catalogued on Wikipedia, alongside its near-duplicate crowd-survey cousin [1]. No date in our sources fixes when the name entered use; it is undocumented here, and English speakers meet it only through the xkcd 2010 survey's close relative, "Dark Mustard," a Delta-E of 5.2 away [1]. The nearest colors on file are [[pinchbeck-brown]] and [[pinchbeck-brown]], both under 4.5 units from this hex [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this tone, as photographed, in 1,232 of 23,781 paintings, 5.18 percent; within a single canvas it is a distinct area in 898 of them, more common than 89 percent of our named colors [2]. Fritz Thomsen is its most devoted painter, using it in 6 of 18 works here, 6.9 times the baseline rate of the museums those paintings come from [2]. It peaks in the 1400s, at 5.2 percent of that century's 945 paintings, and inside a painting it most often plays an accent across its 898 appearances [2]. The earliest dated match is a 1240 panel by the Master of the Cross 434; the archive's early centuries are thin, so this is a floor, not a first, and a color match in an aged photograph is not proof of any dye or pigment [2].
